source.title: Hyperplane Arrangements of Trained ConvNets Are Biased
source.authors: Matteo Gamba; S. Carlsson; Hossein Azizpour; Mårten Björkman

record.tranche_reason: Measures a different trained-network statistic and reports how it relates to learning and validation performance; it does not test the specific interventions or measurements in V1–V8.
record.gate_note: The paper reports projection statistics and weight-reinitialization effects. The statistics are shown in figures; textual descriptions support only qualitative results. Cited results from Zhang et al. are not recorded as this study's own findings.
record.test_reason: The study measures convolutional hyperplane projection bias and layer criticality, neither of which is a measure named by V1–V8. Its noisy-label experiment tracks projection bias during fitting but does not establish the matched natural-label versus random-label generalization comparison required by V1.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors find projection bias associated with learning dynamics and, for large networks on lower-complexity datasets, with layers critical to validation performance. They suggest these configurations may inform understanding of implicit bias and capacity control; they do not establish a generalization-gap predictor or causal explanation.
record.recipe_differences: Measures hyperplane projection statistics and layer criticality rather than testing the listed interventions or generalization measures. Uses SGD with momentum 0.9, weight decay 0.0005, and standard image-classification training setups.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset complexity, layer, training progress, and learning-rate schedule change the projection statistics; pixel representation and disruption of spatial information are also examined in supplemental experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: Projection bias emerges during successful training, including noisy-label fitting, remains unchanged in a failed training run, and changes direction in some ImageNet layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Convolutional filter projection bias tracks aspects of fitting and training dynamics.

fits_no_version.finding: Strong projection bias is associated with layers whose reinitialization harms performance on CIFAR10; learning-rate schedules affect bias and the size of that harm.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Layer projection bias can identify performance-critical layers in some convolutional networks, with dependence on dataset and training schedule.

record.problems: Many outcomes are shown only in figures and reported qualitatively; the stated correlation with generalization is not a direct measurement of train–test error gap. Accuracy on the test set is not reported; the paper says it differs by at most 1% from validation accuracy for all experiments.
record.rows_left_out: No results omitted. Several supplemental figure comparisons are represented as qualitative rows because exact values are not stated in the text.

untested.parts: Matched training recipes demonstrating near-perfect random-label fitting, above-chance natural-label held-out accuracy, and chance random-label held-out accuracy.
Width sweeps beyond zero training error and their effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that recover held-out performance.
Dropout effects on held-out error and their dependence on data size, configuration, and augmentation.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its association with generalization gaps, and comparison with norm- and margin-based measures.
Test accuracy after removing examples selected by memorization influence versus random removal.

record.verdict_notes: All six rows concern constructs outside V1–V8. Their states are therefore cannot_determine relative to these versions, without disputing the reported projection results. Supplemental results on CIFAR100, pixel shuffling, and first-layer representations also fit no version and do not require missing entries for this verdict.

versions.untested_parts: Does not compare natural-label and random-label test accuracy or test the stated architectures and training recipes.
No width sweep or test-error measurement.
No comparison of convolutional and fully connected networks.
Measures projection bias and its association with layer criticality, not magnitude-aware sharpness or the ranking of generalization gaps against norm- and margin-based measures.
Does not remove training examples selected by memorization influence.

rows.subject: AlexNet
rows.operation_detail: Measured the cumulative density of negative projections across convolutional layers during training.
rows.measure: Projection distribution shifted toward negative values in every layer except the first; during training, layers beyond the first shifted from about 50% negative projections toward all-negative projections.
rows.baseline: At initialization, cosine-angle inner products are described as normally distributed with zero mean; layers start with a mixed distribution (∼50% negative projections).
rows.value: After convergence, distributions shifted toward negative values for all layers except the first.
rows.note: The text describes the direction of the figure results but gives no exact final percentages.
rows.check: The reported projection shift is supported by the text but cannot establish any claim version.

rows.subject: VGG19
rows.stage_stated: trained on CIFAR10 with 100% noisy labels
rows.operation_detail: Tracked cumulative density of negative projections during training.

conditions.value: data augmentation and weight decay disabled

rows.measure: Projection statistics were largely unbiased while training loss was approximately constant; around epoch 20, layers 2–5 became more biased as training loss started decreasing.
rows.baseline: Early epochs with approximately constant training loss; statistics described as largely unbiased.
rows.value: Around epoch 20, layers 2–5 started assuming more biased configurations.
rows.note: The paper says this pattern appears to correlate with fitting the data; exact projection values are not stated.
rows.check: Projection bias accompanying noisy-label fitting does not measure the coexistence comparison in V1. The text reports decreasing training loss, without readable final training and held-out accuracy values.

rows.subject: VGG19
rows.stage_stated: trained for 10 epochs on ImageNet; failed to converge
rows.operation_detail: Tracked cumulative density of negative projections during training with weights initialized from N (0, 10−2).
rows.measure: For the last 8 convolutional layers, cumulative density remained constant at 50%; similar behavior was reported for the first 8 layers but not shown.
rows.value: Constant at 50% for the last 8 convolutional layers; similar behavior for the first 8 layers was not shown.
rows.note: The authors report constant training and validation loss for the failed run; the first-eight-layer result is not displayed.
rows.check: Unchanged projection statistics in a failed training run do not establish absence of any V1–V8 effect.

rows.subject: VGG19
rows.operation_detail: Compared projection statistics by layer with layer criticality assessed through weight reinitialization.
rows.measure: Layers 2–8 were described as heavily biased and critical to performance; the remaining convolutional layers could be reset to initialization without considerable performance loss.
rows.baseline: For criticality, corresponding layer weights reset to their value at initialization; for projection statistics, random initialization.
rows.value: The paper reports the association of strong projection bias with layers critical to performance, especially layers 2–8.
rows.note: Performance loss values are not stated in the text; the paper reports the qualitative association.
rows.check: Layer reinitialization sensitivity and projection bias measure neither magnitude-aware sharpness nor train–test gap ranking in V7. Section 3.1 reports validation performance, although Figure 2 calls its outcome test accuracy; retain this source inconsistency.

rows.subject: VGG19
rows.operation_detail: Tracked projection statistics by layer across training.
rows.measure: Early training showed strong negative-projection bias in almost all layers; toward the end, layers 2, 6, and 7 showed strong bias toward positive projections. The paper reports 82% training accuracy for VGG19.
rows.baseline: Early epochs: strong bias toward negative projections in almost all layers.
rows.value: Toward the end, layers 2, 6, and 7 showed strong bias toward positive projections; training accuracy reached 82%.
rows.note: The text links the shift to accommodation of harder patterns but says the training loss plateaus during epochs 30–50.
rows.check: The positive-projection shift and 82% training accuracy do not measure any version. A change in projection direction is not a partial generalization effect.

rows.subject: VGG19
rows.operation_detail: Compared projection statistics across learning-rate schedules.
rows.measure: The step schedule reduced variance across runs and better separated strongly biased layers; the smooth schedule corresponded to less bias and smaller performance drops under weight reinitialization.
rows.value: Exponential schedule: less projection bias and smaller performance drops under weight reinitialization; average number of critical layers was the same.
rows.note: This is a qualitative comparison; exact values are not stated.
rows.check: Learning-rate schedule effects on projection bias and reinitialization sensitivity do not measure any version. This is not an adaptive-optimizer comparison.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
